lighting.environment: dark empty gallery, near-black walls, dark polished concrete floor, no windows, no bright fixtures

key.direction: low raking light from left grazing the terraced foam steps, nearly parallel to the block faces, flagged off the background

lighting.setup: single flagged raking side key in a dark gallery, low fill, no rim

imperfections: clinging foam beads on the ball-end mill
materials.role: machine presence, secondary, out of focus at right edge

imperfections: faint white dust film on frame edges
materials.role: slim black frame of the cropped glass panel

plausibility_notes: clean brushed steel would sit near 0.5 reflectivity; 0.3 with roughness 0.6 accounts for the foam powder film, and pushing it lower would read as painted rather than metal
anisotropy 0.35 meets the brushed-metal rule; dust mutes the grain, so higher values would give implausibly clean streak highlights
the out-of-focus tool head will show mostly as soft dull grey forms; its imperfections are low priority and need not resolve
blackened steel frame at 0.12 reflectivity avoids specular lines that could resolve into figures in the glass
the floor's single chair reflection comes from the polished concrete in the environment and subject text, not from a metal material
a raking key nearly parallel to the block faces maximises shadow relief on the terraces; a frontal key would flatten the foam toward plastic or marble
rationale: Only real metal is parameterised; the foam's matte, dry, granular look is carried by the subject description, so no metal vocabulary can leak onto the chair. The tool head is materials[0] because it is the element most at risk of vanishing, and without it the chair reads as hand-carved. It is brushed steel, but its reflectivity is pulled well below clean brushed steel and its roughness raised to model a powder film: it should read as a working machine coated in the material it removes, not as a polished product. Anisotropy is kept at 0.35, just above the brushed-metal threshold, so the grain shows faintly through the dust without turning into streaked highlights. The vitrine frame is blackened steel, close to non-reflective, so it outlines the glass without adding glints. No chrome or mirror finish appears anywhere: nothing should compete with the foam as a light-bearing surface. The key is a low raking side light from the left that grazes the terraced roughing steps, so form comes from the light/shadow cadence across the steps and not from surface sheen. Matte foam has no specular lobe, so medium hardness gives crisp step shadows without glints. A softer key would flatten the terraces, while a harder one would make the chip scatter look like gravel. At 4300K the light is a neutral-to-slightly-warm gallery tone that keeps the foam chalk-white rather than bluish (snow) or creamy (stone). Low fill at about 8:1 keeps the shadow sides of the chair readable while leaving the gallery near-black. Rim light is off: a rim on white foam reads as a glow, and on glass it would draw bright edge lines.
